However kela + proper noun is a pidgin feature and the text as a whole is rich in pidgin features. The relatively high density of lexifier retentions is probably due to the early date of the text.)

clean.tx: Makou hapai no keia papa.
clean.tl: Let's carry this board of lumber.' (Although makou is the exclusive form in the lexifier, it is here used with inclusive reference. INTENS=intensifier)

clean.tx: Wau puhi kela paka kikalika.

clean.tx: Mahope iaia pimai, pehea ka manawa, hola ahia?
clean.tl: When does he usually come home, at what hour?' (The answer to this question was, 'Sometimes he comes in the afternoon, sometimes he comes in the evening'. Here hola ahia and pehea ka manawa appear to be interchangeable.)

clean.tx: Lapule hola ahia pau hana?
clean.tl: On Sunday, at what hour was the work finished?' (Ahia usually means 'how many' in Hawaiian and the pidgin, but the question is not how long the work will take because the answer to the question was Hola 9 '9 o'clock'. Hola ahia thus specifies a specific time and not a duration. See Examples 34 and 38 as well.)

clean.tx: Pehea iaia keia manawa, pehea kela ma‘i iaia?

clean.tx: Henry huipu wau inu akahi omole.

clean.tx: Wau me Ah Tini So noho ma ka lumi paina.
clean.tl: Ah Tini So and I were in the dining room.

clean.tx: Mahope hele aku maua me Kauiaa.
clean.tl: Later Kauiaa and I left (the house).' (There are no examples in the corpus, but the pattern in this example (taken from court testimony of a Hawaiian speaker code-switching into Pidgin Hawaiian in the same sentence) is the usual pattern in the lexifier and was probably at least an option in the pidgin.)

clean.tl: You had better leave, and don't do that. OR: You had better get off from here, and don't do that.' (The first translation is adapted from the source. The second is the translation given in the source material.)

clean.tl: I don't want to sell this chicken.

clean.tx: Iaia hele no a ki no aha kani kela pu, kela kani akahi, alua, aole ku, kela kani akolu wau ku no ma ka uha, wau hina ma ke alanui.
clean.tl: He came and shot his gun four times; after the first and second shots I no longer was standing and at the third shot I got up on my knees and fell into the street.

clean.tl: Five times I went over to his house.

clean.tl: That black one is mine.' (In Hawaiian, ponoi is not verbal 'own', but 'own' as in 'my own'. The translation has been adapted from the official court translation.)

clean.tx: Lanai maikai, Lahaina aole maikai.
clean.tl: Lanai is better than Lahaina (as a place to dock). OR: Lanai is good, Lahaina is not good.' (This was said by a captain approaching the port of Lahaina who decided to sail to the nearby island Lanai where the sea was calmer.)

clean.tx: Olelo hou ana.
clean.tl: [He] was speaking again.

clean.tx: Oe mamua aie akahi dala, aole hoihoi mai, wau aole makana akahi dala iaoe.
clean.tl: You previously borrowed a dollar that you never returned to me, so I'm not going to give you a dollar.

clean.tx: Wau hoi no mamua ma kela hale iaia.
clean.tl: I indeed went back previously to his house.

clean.tx: Aole wau manao make ana wau, aka, wau nui loa eha keia manawa.
clean.tl: I didn't think I was dying but I was in a lot of pain at the time.' (Make is a stative (neuter) verb in Hawaiian and here it appears to refer to the process or state of dying.)

clean.tx: Pehea ia Wainui makemake ana?
clean.tl: What does Wainui want?' (The ia in this example does not have a clear gloss; its presence is possibly due to exaggeration.)

clean.tx: Ma Nawiliwili au noho nana ka halekuai, ma Hulaia kekahi manawa nana kela mahi laiki.
clean.tl: At Nawiliwili I usually watch the store, at Hulaia I sometimes watch over the rice plantation.

clean.tx: Wau noho hana kamana ma ka mahiko o Makaweli ma nehinei.
clean.tl: I was working in carpentry at Makaweli sugar plantation yesterday.' (It is ambiguous whether hana here is a noun or a verb and whether there is a nominal (hana kamana) or verbal (noho hana) compound. The lexifier has the latter as a compound (e.g. noho hana 'ole, 'to be unemployed').)

clean.tx: Pehea pauloa manawa makemake ike Edita?
clean.tl: Why do you usually want to see Edith?

clean.tx: Aole hiki wau malama kela ohana wau pauloa manawa.
clean.tl: I usually was unable to care for my family.

clean.tx: Wau kamailio pololei ka mea pau oe kamailio.
clean.tl: I'll tell [him] accurately what you've told me.

clean.tx: Pehea oe molowa wikiwiki?
clean.tl: Why have you suddenly become tired?

clean.tx: Makawela hanapaa kela puu, wau aole hiki hele mawaho, wau kahea holina.
clean.tl: Makawela grabbed my throat, I couldn't go outside, I called for help.

clean.tx: Oe paha panipani kela wahine au!
clean.tl: Maybe you slept with my wife!

clean.tx: Iaia lawe paha aole paha, aole wau ike.
clean.tl: Maybe he took it, maybe not, I don't know.

clean.tx: Aole oe hopu, makou piliwaiwai.
clean.tl: Don't arrest [us], we [would like to] gamble. OR: Don’t you make any arrest. You let us gamble. (official court translation)' (Makou here is exclusive plural.)

clean.tx: Wau aole nana kela mau poho kiwi.
clean.tl: I didn't look at the bullhorn containers.

clean.tx: Ku malie oe, oe malama, oe ku!
clean.tl: Stand still, watch out, stop!

clean.tx: Mai walaau oe!
clean.tl: Don't talk!

clean.tx: Aole wau pepehi kela kepani.
clean.tl: I didn't beat up that Japanese.

clean.tx: Pehea oe aihue i ka dala?
clean.tl: Why did you steal the dollar?

clean.tx: Oe aihue kela hua wau, oe ule pilau!
clean.tl: You stole my fruit, you scumbag!

clean.tx: Akahi keiki pukiki lawe akahi dala ulaula.
clean.tl: A Portuguese kid took a gold dollar.

clean.tx: Poakahi ahiahi kela, aole maopopo ka hora ia‘u.
clean.tl: That was on Monday evening, I don't recall the hour.' (Maopopo is a neuter verb in Hawaiian; the patient-like subject (unmarked with case morphology) is 'the hour' whereas the agent is a not a core argument marked with the objective/oblique marker (hence the verb is intransitive). The sentence may be paraphrased as 'the hour is not in the state of being known (by me)'.)

clean.tx: Elua lumi liilii umi Iapana moemoe maloko.
clean.tl: Ten Japanese were sleeping inside two little rooms.' (This is an example of an intransitive that is not a neuter verb, with an agentive subject.)

clean.tx: Wau hina ma ke alanui.
clean.tl: I fell into the street.' (Hina is a neuter verb, and thus has a patient-like subject.)

clean.tx: Iaia hana hina ia'u malolo
clean.tl: He threw me down.' (Hanahina is a pidgin innovation; hina 'fall' is a neuter verb and prefixation with hana- 'make, do' transitivizes it; the Hawaiian equivalent is ho'ohina. This sentence is thus transitive. The use of case marking is more common with early texts. Iaia for third person singular is not an instance of case-marking, as it occurs obligatorily for both subjects and objects.)

clean.tx: Wau pimai no ma Sana Miguela.
clean.tl: I come from São Miguel.' (Pi mai ‘come’ is spelled without a space in the analyzed text to yield a one-to-correspondence between morpheme and gloss. It is almost always spelled with a space in extant sources and thus appears with this conventional spelling in the published literature on Pidgin Hawaiian. Although mai is analyzable as a directional, pi never occurs alone as a basic motion verb ‘go’ or ‘come’.)

clean.tx: Wau makana keia upena kela haole.
clean.tl: I gave this net to the white foreigner.' (The more common order in Pidgin Hawaiian is recipient + theme as opposed to the order found here.)

clean.tx: Iaia lawe mai haawi ia Henry alua omole.
clean.tl: He brought and gave two bottles to Henry.

clean.tx: Mahope wau makana kela haku kela dala.
clean.tl: Then I gave the boss the money.

clean.tx: Kela wahine kela Amala haawi no ka rama.
clean.tl: That woman gave Amala the liquor. OR: That woman Amala gave the liquor (to X).' (Without checking the original record, I am uncertain which is the correct interpretation. However the first translation is more likely to be correct, as kela wahine Amala is more typical for the latter translation and the lack of a recipient is a difficulty. INTENS=intensifier)

clean.tx: Mahope wau makemake kamailio Koolau, mahope Ø hele makai, wau makemake nana Ø, pehea la?
clean.tl: I want to talk to Koolau soon, so [when he gets back] he can then come down seaward [to where I will be]. I want to see him, is that okay?

clean.tx: Wau manao akahi pihi nui iaia paani kela wai.
clean.tl: I thought that a huge fish was playing in the water. (describing the characteristics of a loud sound made during a landslide) OR: It seemed as if a huge fish were playing in the water. OR: It sounded like what a huge fish playing in the water would sound like.

clean.tx: Alima moa loaa kela hale iaia.
clean.tl: There were five chickens at his house. OR: Five chickens were found at his house.' (It must be noted that the existential verb loaa is a neuter verb in the lexifier, so alima moa is properly the grammatical subject (i.e. five chickens collectively is the entity that is in the state of existence) if loaa is still a neuter verb in the pidgin. Grammatical relations were variable in Pidgin neuter verbs; in many cases the subject of loaa in its possessive non-existential sense is the possessor, not the possessed (which is the subject in the lexifier, as this is the entity in the state of possession).)

clean.tx: Ma kahi o ka pake, loaa kela wahine pake ma ka lanai.
clean.tl: At the Chinese place, there was a Chinese woman on the verandah.

clean.tx: Nui loa ka ua a me ka wai.
clean.tl: There is a lot of rain and water. OR: It's raining heavily (and the river is flooding).

clean.tx: Kela ua pimai.
clean.tl: It is raining.' (This is a hypothetical example based on the typical raining construction of early Hawai'i Pidgin English (rain come). It is unclear whether Pidgin Hawaiian used the same pattern, but the attested pattern in Example 113 does utilize the noun 'rain' as opposed to the verb, as is the case here.)

clean.tx: Kela poo eha no.
clean.tl: [My] head is in pain.' (This example is constructed from: Kela Kipau hahau kela poo, eha no (own data, 1885), 'Kipau whipped my head, [and it] was pained'. But here eha lacks an overt subject. However it conforms to the form of other statements about body parts in pain in the data (see Example 117) and it also conforms to Example 116 which does concern a headache per se. INTENS=intensifier.)

clean.tx: Mauka ga pilikia.
clean.tl: I have a headache.' (This is from a complaint by a Japanese field labourer of having a headache during her period. However the example is not pure Pidgin Hawaiian but represents a mixed variety of Pidgin Hawaiian and Hawai'i Pidgin English (ga is a topic marker from Japanese). Here mauka, usually a directional referring towards the mountains, is used with the pidginized sense of 'above' as a circumlocution for the 'head'.)

clean.tx: Eha opu.
clean.tl: I have a bellyache.' (Note that here the word order is verb-subject. This word order was most common with neuter verbs like eha.)

clean.tx: Ia makainana pau loa ia aole makemake ia Wainui Kuhina.
clean.tl: The commoners don't like the prime minister (or minister of finance).' (This text contains an exaggerated and meaningless repetition of the objective/oblique marker. There is also a pun on the titles of kuhina nui 'prime minister' and kuhina waiwai 'minister of finance', via wai nui 'drool'.)

clean.tx: Wau nui makau.
clean.tl: I'm very afraid.

clean.tx: Akahi hamale wau inaha pauloa puniu.
clean.tl: With a hammer I smash every skull. OR: My hammer smashes every skull.' (This sentence is ambiguous on account of the pronominal possessive construction.)

clean.tx: Kipau hana eha wau, me ka pu hana eha iaia wau.
clean.tl: Kipau injured me, with his gun he injured me.

clean.tx: Aole laau wau hahau iaia.
clean.tl: I didn't strike him with a stick. OR: It wasn't a stick with which I struck him.' (The first translation more likely represents the sense because the narrative up to this point does not mention that the speaker struck his attacker, whereas it was his attacker who hit him. So it is more probable that the speaker is here denying any allegation that he hit his attacker. In both cases, laau designates an instrument used in an act of hitting.)

clean.tx: Wau ike kela Moaka hele mai me ka pahi.
clean.tl: I saw Moaka coming with his knife.

clean.tx: Wau me Ah Tini So, Aho, noho ma ka lumi paina.
clean.tl: Ah Tini So, Aho, and I were in the dining room.

clean.tx: George Bell Jr. a me Kawai hele malalo.
clean.tl: George Bell Jr. and Kawai went down.' (The space between a me is a spelling convention where a morpheme boundary is shown by a space, but where the two elements correspond to a single English word. So a me is literally "and with", but it is the basic coordinator for noun phrases ("and").)

clean.tx: Maua halawai me Naukana.
clean.tl: The two of us met with Naukana.

clean.tx: Henry huipu wau inu akahi omole.
clean.tl: Henry and I drank one bottle (of beer).

clean.tx: Wau mamua pii maluna a nana lakou puhi no.
clean.tl: I previously climbed up and watched them smoke.

clean.tx: Oe malihini.
clean.tl: You're a tourist (not a resident).

clean.tx: Kela poo liilii ano poepoe.
clean.tl: The [mare's] head is somewhat small and round.

clean.tx: Akahi Japani noho ma kela hale pake!
clean.tl: A Japanese is at the Chinese house!

clean.tx: Pehea la kanaka ma kela hale wau?
clean.tl: Why is that person at my house?

clean.tx: Oe loaa pihi no?
clean.tl: Do you have any fish? (as inquired by a prospective customer)' (Loaa is a neuter verb in Hawaiian (with the meaning 'to be obtained, possessed'), but often in Pidgin Hawaiian it occurs with the possessor in preverbal subject position. Since fish are obtained via fishing, it is possible that meaning is not that of a simple possessive. INTENS=intensifier)

clean.tx: Kela Moaka akahi pahi, kela Kipau akahi pu.
clean.tl: Moaka had a knife, Kipau had a gun.

clean.tx: Loaa nuinui lole maikai loa ma Hale Keokeo, helu 31, alanui Nuuanu.
clean.tl: There are lots of very nice clothes at the White House, 31 Nuuanu St.

clean.tx: Kanaka pauloa hele Kauai.
clean.tl: Everyone went to Kauai.

clean.tx: Wau makemake hele ma Hanalei.
clean.tl: I want to go to Hanalei.

clean.tx: Loaa mai no palapala mai Kina mai iaia aole hele ma Kina.
clean.tl: I received a letter from China [to the effect that] he didn't go to China.' (Here loaa is used as a neuter verb with the sense of 'received, obtained'. DIR=directional, INTENS=intensifier)

clean.tx: Wau hele ma kela hale wau.
clean.tl: I went to my house.

clean.tx: Wau pimai no ma Sana Miguela.
clean.tl: I come from Saõ Miguel.

clean.tx: Kokoke 10 minute hiki mai Laumana mai ka halekuke mai.
clean.tl: About ten minutes later Laumana returned from the kitchen.

clean.tx: Wau no moe malalo.
clean.tl: I rested (on the bed) below.

clean.tx: Makawela hanapaa hou kela puu wau, kulai ma ke kuauna.
clean.tl: Makawela grabbed my throat again and shoved [me] into the river bank.

clean.tx: Akahi kepani kulai ia‘u hina malalo o ka lepo.
clean.tl: A Japanese pushed me down into the ground.

clean.tx: Kela ekolu kepani hanapaa kela pake hina malalo.
clean.tl: Three Japanese held the Chinese down.' (Although the semantics are not identical with the word for 'push', the sense of 'hold down' is similar.)

clean.tx: Lalau kela poo au kulai malalo.
clean.tl: [He] grabbed my head and pushed it down.

clean.tx: Kawai paa kela Lauman ala maluna.
clean.tl: Kawai pulled Lauman up (from his bed). OR: Kawai grabbed Lauman and [he] rose up (from his bed).' (It is unclear whether a serial verb construction is involved here, but it seems quite plausible.)

clean.tx: Hele kokua kela pake ala maluna.
clean.tl: I went to help the Chinese get up.' (The word 'pull' is not used but kokua ala 'help get up' is a similar concept.)

clean.tx: Oukou hapai wau huipu Kakina maluna kela kua.
clean.tl: You pull Kakina and I up from our backs.' (The sentence is metaphorical in terms of social betterment.)

clean.tx: Oe aole pono kau maluna o kela lio.
clean.tl: You shouldn't mount my horse.

clean.tx: Oe ike kela dala kela pukiki poina maluna kela pahu?
clean.tl: Did you see the money that the Portuguese left on the box?

clean.tx: Moaka lawe kela wahine ia Kipau hele ma Koloa.
clean.tl: Moaka took Kipau's wife away to Koloa.

clean.tx: Mahope kela Kepani kii mai hopu iaia hele.
clean.tl: Then the Japanese took him away.

clean.tx: Pehea oe loihi hele pimai?
clean.tl: Why did it take so long for you to come?

clean.tx: Iaia kii kela beer haawi Henry Moore.
clean.tl: He fetched some beer for Henry Moore. OR: He fetched some beer to give to Henry Moore.' (Note that the same speaker produced Example 157 in the same speech event.)

clean.tx: Iaia lawe mai haawi ia Henry alua omole.
clean.tl: He brought two bottles for Henry. OR: He brought and gave Henry two bottles.

clean.tx: Wau olelo akahi kao malama iaia kino.
clean.tl: I told a lazy fellow to take care of himself.

clean.tx: Oe makana wau $1 akahi la, a wau kaukau mi.
clean.tl: Pay me a dollar per day and I will feed myself.' (Note that the reflexive pronoun is a borrowing from Hawai'i Pidgin English and is distinct in form from the usual 1SG pronoun used in the same sentence.)

clean.tx: Wau no ike keia pake, Ta Mon inoa iaia.
clean.tl: I (indeed) saw this Chinese, Ta Mon is his name.

clean.tx: Wau hele no ma kela wahi Kapule.
clean.tl: I went (indeed) to Kapule's place.

clean.tx: Kalo huhu wau, wau huhu iaia.
clean.tl: Kalo and I became angry with each other.

clean.tx: Laua huki ka lauoho laua.
clean.tl: The two of them pulled each other's hair.

clean.tx: Aole kela ka lole aihue ia.
clean.tl: Those are not the clothes which were stolen.' (Notice that this sentence also contains a subject relative clause. Passives with 'ia are very rare in the pidgin.)

clean.tx: Kela ten dollars makana au, oe kipu au?
clean.tl: Those ten dollars that were given to me, (was that so) you could bribe me? OR: Did you give me that $10 as bribe money? (official court translation)' (The official translation is non-literal (e.g. 'bribe' is the main verb, not an nominal modifier).)

clean.tx: Iaia aihue ke dala [Ø __ haawi iaia makana kela makua wau].
clean.tl: He stole the money that was given to him to give to my father.

clean.tx: Mahope akahi pake holo mai, kela Makawela hanapaa wau kui wau ma ka umauma wau, mahope kela pake holo mai hemo kela puka wau holo mawaho.
clean.tl: Then a Chinese (outside the house) ran to me, as Makawela held me punching my chest; then the Chinese who was running to me opened the door, and I ran outside.

clean.tx: Keia ka pake panipani ia'u.
clean.tl: This is the Chinese who raped me.

clean.tx: Iaia pimai, wau kamailio pololei ka mea pau oe kamailio.
clean.tl: When he comes, I'll tell him exactly what you said.

clean.tx: Keia pu no ka pu a Kipau i ki ai iau.
clean.tl: This is the gun with which Kipau shot me.' (This is a sentence in non-pidginized Hawaiian that comes at the end of a speaker's testimony in the pidgin (probably reflecting code switching). The sentence shares case marking and the relative clause construction with the lexifier. The Pidgin equivalent may well be keia ka pu Kipau mamua ki wau [this DEF gun Kipau before shoot 1SG].)

clean.tx: Keia ka pu Kipau mamua ki wau.
clean.tl: This is the gun with which Kipau shot me.' (This is a hypothetical constructed example based on Example 171.)

clean.tx: Oe olelo wau likepu baby.
clean.tl: You said that I'm like a baby.

clean.tx: Pehea oe kamailio oe hele moemoe?
clean.tl: Why did you say that you were going to sleep?

clean.tx: Wau manao oe kolohe kela lio wau.
clean.tl: I think you injured my horse.

clean.tx: Wau ike iaia noho ma Hulaia.
clean.tl: I know that he lives in Hulaia.

clean.tx: Wau aole makemake kuai keia moa.
clean.tl: I do not want to sell this chicken.

clean.tx: Kela aliikoa makemake wau kiola mawaho kela ipukapa.
clean.tl: The military officer wanted me to toss it outside the gate.

clean.tx: Wau aole panipani kela Napumala.
clean.tl: I didn't rape Napumala.

clean.tx: Aole kanaka nana, ma ka puka aniani.
clean.tl: Nobody saw [this] at the window.

clean.tx: Aole hana keia la, la nui Moi, aole hana kanaka.
clean.tl: There is no work today, it's a royal holiday, nobody works.

clean.tx: Bia no [kela mea maua inu].
clean.tl: Beer is what we drank.

clean.tx: Oe [ka mea pepehi kela wahine oe].
clean.tl: You're the one who beat your wife.

clean.tx: Henry akahi kiaha me hapa, wau likepu no.
clean.tl: Henry had a glass and a half (of beer), I too [had a glass and a half].' (like pu is always spelled with a space, but functionally it is a unit.)

clean.tx: E Joe, pimai nana kela lio oe!
clean.tl: Joe, come look at your horse!

clean.tx: Olelo oe wau pikanene hikino oe pono olelo wau pikanene.
clean.tl: You called me a child, okay you should call me a child.

clean.tx: Iaia lawe kela opiuma, komo ka paiki wau, nanao no kela lima iaia loaa no kela opiuma.
clean.tl: He took my opium; he entered my pocket by thrusting his hand inside, finding the opium.

clean.tx: Iaia eha kela manamana kela mahina September […] kokoke akahi mahina eha kela lima.
clean.tl: He hurt his fingers back in September […] almost for a month his hand hurt.' (The context makes it clear that fingers are what manamana denotes here.)

clean.tx: Poakahi aole loaa hulu moa ma kela hale oe?
clean.tl: On Monday were any chicken feathers found at your house?

clean.tx: Laua huki ka lauoho laua.
clean.tl: They pulled each other's hair.

clean.tx: hulu
clean.tl: body hair/feathers' (Unfortunately, there are no clear references to body hair in the corpus, just head hair. The lexifier however has a distinct term for head hair (lauoho) and the same term for body hair and feathers (hulu), so it is possible that this overlap was retained in Pidgin Hawaiian.)

clean.tx: honi
clean.tl: smell

clean.tx: Wau lohe kela wai nuinui walaau.
clean.tl: I heard the water make a chattering sound.

clean.tx: Kela wa pau hakaka, iaia piimai no kela hale maomao.
clean.tl: When [he] was done fighting, he came to the green house.' (This is probably not a reference to a greenhouse (the term for which in the lexifier is hale ho'oūlu mea kanu), but it is not impossible.)

clean.tx: Nana kela moa wahine eleele malalo o ka hale o Lau Chee.
clean.tl: I saw that black hen under Lau Chee’s house. (official court translation)

clean.tx: Owau olelo Kaluaokahaku hana papapala no, lio keokeo wahine kuai me ka haole.
clean.tl: I told Kaluaokahaku to make a document (regarding) the white mare (which) would be sold to the white person. OR: I told Kaluaokahaku to make a deed for the sale of my white mare to the haole. (official court translation)

clean.tx: Mahea oe waiho kela eke palani oe?
clean.tl: Where did you leave your sack of bran?

clean.tx: Iaia aole loaa akahi balota.
clean.tl: He won't receive a single vote (in the election).

clean.tx: Wau makemake kue Pake hanahana hamabuga.
clean.tl: I want to oppose the Chinese by making trouble. OR: I want to oppose the Chinese who make trouble.' (Hamabuga is a borrowing from Hawai'i Pidgin English and it takes the place of Hawaiian pilikia. It was rare in Pidgin Hawaiian and it also is rare in Hawai'i Pidgin English, where pilikia was the dominant word for indicating 'trouble, problem'.)

clean.tx: Akolu pake wau aha ma kela hale, makou limalima kela rumi, Aiau kela hale.
clean.tl: Three Chinese and I, four total, were in that house; we rented rooms at Aiau's house.

clean.tx: Wau lohe no kani […] wau holoi lole kela manawa.
clean.tl: I heard a sound […] I was washing clothes at the time (i.e. at the time when I heard a sound).

orig.tl: I heard a sound […] I was washing clothes at the time (i.e. at the time when I heard a sound).

clean.tx: Oe hiki no nana iaia a kamailio kela manao oe.
clean.tl: You could see him and tell [him] your thoughts.

clean.tx: Wau paa mamua halepaahao.
clean.tl: I was previously imprisoned.' (Paa is a neuter verb, the default value of which is stative (less often it expresses changes of state). Here the verb has past reference.)

clean.tx: Aie akahi dala.
clean.tl: [I want to] borrow a dollar [from you].' (Aie is a dynamic verb, and here it is used with non-past reference.)

clean.tx: Kela haole maluna kela moku [kela mea wau kokua].
clean.tl: It was the white person aboard the ship whom I helped.' (In my notes, kela occurs without mea. This could represent either a reduction from kela mea or an omission on the part of the court reporter.)

flagged.tl: himself/herself' (Of the Hawaiian directionals (which syntactically follow the verb), only mai 'hither' is used productively in the pidgin; iho 'down' is used only twice (usually the preposition malalo, which means 'bottom' in the lexifier, is used for this function). Iho was also used to indicate the reflexive, whether as a verbal modifier (directional 'down') or more commonly as a pronominal modifier. This was the most common method of indicating the reflexive in the lexifier, so it is possible that the same strategy was used at least in part in the pidgin. Since reflexives are so rare in the data, this possibility must be kept open.)
